topic: Design the sync layer for an offline-first note-taking app used by teams.

shared_context.goal: Design the sync layer for an offline-first note-taking app used by teams.
history: We're still pretending "file merge" is a generic abstraction when the real merge problem is managing concurrent edits across multiple users and devices without forcing users to manually resolve every conflict.
I’m not defending merge algorithms in the abstract; I’m saying the sync layer must record every edit with a verifiable, immutable history so users can audit and restore any version.

I’m not comfortable with immutable history alone, because it makes rollback a one-way door. The sync layer needs a more dynamic approach: record diffs, not snapshots, and surface merge windows before users lose track of who wrote what.

I’m not sold on immutable history plus diffs alone; the point is to make the merge model strong enough that concurrent edits are resolved before they’re ever visible as conflicts. For notes, that means CRDTs plus explicit merge windows—rich-text and attachment edits get processed as operations, not artifacts.

CRDTs plus merge windows sound neat until you admit the merge window is just a human interpretation of the edit graph; if the sync layer doesn’t emit an immutable, queryable version history, every “merge window” just becomes an opaque reconstruction.

I’m not defending a single approach; I’m pushing for a two-level history: immutable diffs for auditability, plus a recoverable merge window that lets users rollback to a mergeable state without sacrificing provenance.

I’m not comfortable with treating merge windows as a side note; they’re the observable face of the merge model. If the sync layer can’t emit a recoverable, user-readable merge history, then it’s not truly handling concurrency—it’s just storing snapshots and calling the result “reconciled.”

A recoverable merge window is fine, but it still leaves a blind spot: if the sync layer can’t prove what happened in the merge, users won’t trust the restored note. The better design is to record an immutable version history with queryable diffs, so every merge is explainable and auditable…

I’m not convinced “immutable history” is the right guardrail here. If the only provable thing is the final merge, you’ve traded auditability for opacity; the better rule is: each edit is recorded and each merge is recorded independently, with a recoverable window and a verifiable diff log.

Teams need auditability and version recovery.
Conflicts should be minimized and not pushed onto users by default.

Recording diffs can preserve change provenance while allowing more flexible rollback.

perspective_map.name: Conflict resolution and consistency model
perspective_map.theory: Sync should be designed around a strong, explicit merge model—such as CRDTs or operational transforms—because the primary cause of sync success is how safely concurrent edits are reconciled without data loss or user-visible conflicts.

perspective_map.name: User trust through data integrity
perspective_map.theory: The sync layer should prioritize immutable versioning, auditability, and recoverability because users will only rely on offline-first collaboration if they can always inspect, restore, and prove what happened to their notes.

perspective_map.name: Latency and perceived responsiveness
perspective_map.theory: The best sync design is one that makes local edits instantaneous and treats server synchronization as background eventual consistency, because responsiveness is the main driver of user satisfaction in offline-first note-taking.

perspective_map.name: Team workflow and collaboration semantics
perspective_map.theory: Sync should be shaped by the real collaborative behaviors of teams—shared notebooks, permissions, commenting, and ownership boundaries—because the main challenge is not transport but preserving social and organizational intent across devices.

perspective_map.name: Operational simplicity and maintainability
perspective_map.theory: The sync layer should be kept deliberately simple, using a narrow data model and straightforward retry logic, because long-term reliability and debuggability matter more than maximizing theoretical concurrency or feature richness.
